It really feels like I'm just moving through a movie of my life rather than actually living it.\n\nDoctor: Can you describe if these feelings of detachment and being in a 'movie' are more distressing or disruptive to your daily life compared to the hypervigilance and fear of something bad happening again?\n\nPatient: It's hard to say which is worse because they both severely damage my daily functioning and overall well-being in different ways. The hypervigilance keeps me constantly tense and avoiding places I need to go for my job, while the out-of-body feeling completely isolates me and stops me from connecting with my family and team. Ultimately, both cause so much disruption to my life that I'm not sure which one is actually causing the greater amount of harm.\n\nDoctor: You've described both hypervigilance and feelings of detachment as severely impacting your daily life. Can you tell me more about how these symptoms have affected your ability to maintain relationships with your family and colleagues?\n\nPatient: With my family, meals have become incredibly tense because I'm constantly on edge and scanning the exits even at my parents' house, which makes them keep asking what's wrong with me. With my colleagues, I feel completely flat and disconnected—I couldn't even share their excitement when we closed a big deal, and my constant scanning during client dinners and avoiding social outings has really strained things with my team and my boss.\n\nDoctor: Have you experienced any significant memory lapses or gaps in your memory for events that occurred after the shooting, aside from the specific moment of the shooting itself?\n\nPatient: No, I don't have any memory gaps for anything that happened after the shooting. I used to be very social, active, and successful at work, but now I just feel flat and unable to feel any real happiness. It honestly feels like I'm watching someone else's life instead of actually living my own.\n\nDoctor: Can you tell me when you first started feeling this sense of detachment and disconnection from yourself and your surroundings, was it immediately after the shooting or did it develop over time?\n\nPatient: It started pretty much right after the shooting, and it’s been going on for the last ten days now. Since that night, everything has felt completely unreal, like voices sound far away, colors look washed out, and I'm just floating outside my own body.\n\nDoctor: You mentioned the feelings of detachment started right after the shooting, ten days ago. Have these feelings of detachment and disconnection from yourself and your surroundings been constant since then, or have they varied in intensity over the past ten days?\n\nPatient: They aren't constant every single second, but they have been happening a lot of the time over the last ten days. It happens very frequently, making me feel like I'm moving through a movie with washed-out colors and distant voices, as if I'm floating outside my own body.\n\nDoctor: You've mentioned that these feelings of detachment and hypervigilance started after the shooting and have been ongoing for the last ten days. Have you noticed any specific triggers that make these symptoms worse or better over the course of a day?\n\nPatient: Sudden loud noises like a car backfiring or a stapler slamming at work instantly trigger intense physical panic, and being in crowded, unpredictable places like busy restaurants makes the hypervigilance and detachment much worse. Honestly, nothing really makes it feel better yet, because even in familiar places like my office or my parents' house, my body won't let me relax and I'm still constantly scanning the exits.\n\nDoctor: You mentioned that the feelings of detachment started right after the shooting and have been ongoing for the last ten days. Do you think these symptoms have been getting worse, better, or staying about the same over the course of these ten days?\n\nPatient: I'm not entirely sure whether they are getting better or worse. Part of me is terrified that this is just how my life is going to be from now on.\n\nDoctor: Do you think your main issue is the intense fear and hypervigilance you're experiencing, or is it more the feeling of being disconnected from yourself and your surroundings that's causing you the most distress?\n\nPatient: It’s hard to choose because both are deeply distressing in different ways; the constant hypervigilance and jumpiness keep me physically exhausted and feeling unsafe everywhere, while the disconnection makes me feel like I’m floating outside my body and unable to engage with my life. I catch myself thinking, \"This can't be real.\"\n\nDoctor: How often do you experience this feeling of being detached from yourself or your surroundings, and does it happen only in response to reminders of the shooting or at other times as well?\n\nPatient: I feel this way a lot of the time lately, and it's not just when I'm reminded of the shooting. It happens even during normal daily routines, where I feel like I'm floating outside my body watching myself go through the motions while people's voices sound distant and colors look washed out. It really feels like I'm just moving through a movie of my life rather than actually living it.\n\nDoctor: Can you describe if these feelings of detachment and being in a 'movie' are more distressing or disruptive to your daily life compared to the hypervigilance and fear of something bad happening again?\n\nPatient: It's hard to say which is worse because they both severely damage my daily functioning and overall well-being in different ways. The hypervigilance keeps me constantly tense and avoiding places I need to go for my job, while the out-of-body feeling completely isolates me and stops me from connecting with my family and team. Ultimately, both cause so much disruption to my life that I'm not sure which one is actually causing the greater amount of harm.\n\nDoctor: You've described both hypervigilance and feelings of detachment as severely impacting your daily life. Can you tell me more about how these symptoms have affected your ability to maintain relationships with your family and colleagues?\n\nPatient: With my family, meals have become incredibly tense because I'm constantly on edge and scanning the exits even at my parents' house, which makes them keep asking what's wrong with me. With my colleagues, I feel completely flat and disconnected—I couldn't even share their excitement when we closed a big deal, and my constant scanning during client dinners and avoiding social outings has really strained things with my team and my boss.\n\nDoctor: Have you experienced any significant memory lapses or gaps in your memory for events that occurred after the shooting, aside from the specific moment of the shooting itself?\n\nPatient: No, I don't have any memory gaps for anything that happened after the shooting. I actually remember everything before and after that night very clearly. The only blank spot or \"black hole\" in my mind is just that specific moment when the shooting actually started.\n\nDoctor: Do you feel like you've changed significantly as a person since the shooting, or that you're no longer the same person you were before it happened?\n\nPatient: Yes, I feel completely disconnected from the person I used to be. I used to be very social, active, and successful at work, but now I just feel flat and unable to feel any real happiness. It honestly feels like I'm watching someone else's life instead of actually living my own.\n\nDoctor: Can you tell me when you first started feeling this sense of detachment and disconnection from yourself and your surroundings, was it immediately after the shooting or did it develop over time?\n\nPatient: It started pretty much right after the shooting, and it’s been going on for the last ten days now. Since that night, everything has felt completely unreal, like voices sound far away, colors look washed out, and I'm just floating outside my own body.\n\nDoctor: You mentioned the feelings of detachment started right after the shooting, ten days ago. Have these feelings of detachment and disconnection from yourself and your surroundings been constant since then, or have they varied in intensity over the past ten days?\n\nPatient: They aren't constant every single second, but they have been happening a lot of the time over the last ten days. It happens very frequently, making me feel like I'm moving through a movie with washed-out colors and distant voices, as if I'm floating outside my own body.\n\nDoctor: You've mentioned that these feelings of detachment and hypervigilance started after the shooting and have been ongoing for the last ten days. Have you noticed any specific triggers that make these symptoms worse or better over the course of a day?\n\nPatient: Sudden loud noises like a car backfiring or a stapler slamming at work instantly trigger intense physical panic, and being in crowded, unpredictable places like busy restaurants makes the hypervigilance and detachment much worse. Honestly, nothing really makes it feel better yet, because even in familiar places like my office or my parents' house, my body won't let me relax and I'm still constantly scanning the exits.\n\nDoctor: You mentioned that the feelings of detachment started right after the shooting and have been ongoing for the last ten days. Do you think these symptoms have been getting worse, better, or staying about the same over the course of these ten days?\n\nPatient: I'm not entirely sure whether they are getting better or worse. The feelings of detachment have just been pretty constant and overwhelming ever since the shooting occurred, so it's hard to tell if there has been any real change.\n\nDoctor: You've been experiencing these symptoms for ten days now, but can you tell me if there have been any periods, even brief ones, where you felt somewhat back to normal or like your old self since the shooting?\n\nPatient: No, I haven't had any moments of feeling back to normal at all. Since the shooting ten days ago, this feeling of being constantly on guard and tense has been continuous. I haven't been able to relax or feel like my old self even for a second.\n\nDoctor: !!!!!Can you tell me if you have experienced any other dissociative symptoms, such as feeling like you are in a daze, or if there are other times when you feel like you are not in control of your actions or thoughts?\n\nPatient: I definitely feel like I am in a constant daze, almost like I'm moving through a movie of my life rather than actually living it. It feels like I'm floating outside my own body watching myself go through the motions and thinking \"this can't be real,\" while people's voices sound distant and colors look washed out. I wouldn't say I feel out of control of my actions, but that dazed, disconnected feeling is definitely there.\n\nDoctor: You've been experiencing dissociative symptoms for ten days now, but can you tell me if you think these symptoms would persist even if you were in a safe and completely relaxed environment, or do you think they would decrease significantly in such a setting?\n\nPatient: I'm honestly not sure because right now, it's incredibly hard for me to even imagine what feeling completely safe and relaxed would be like. Since my body won't let me experience that, I really don't know if these feelings of detachment would actually go away or not.\n\nDoctor: You've been experiencing these symptoms for ten days now, but do you think if you were given more time, say a few more weeks or months, these feelings of detachment and hypervigilance might decrease on their own, or do you feel like they're becoming a more permanent part of your life?\n\nPatient: I'm really not sure because it's only been ten days, but right now everything is so intense that it's hard to imagine it just going away on its own. Part of me is terrified that this is just how my life is going to be from now on.\n\nDoctor: Do you think your main issue is the intense fear and hypervigilance you're experiencing, or is it more the feeling of being disconnected from yourself and your surroundings that's causing you the most distress?\n\nPatient: It’s hard to choose because both are deeply distressing in different ways; the constant hypervigilance and jumpiness keep me physically exhausted and feeling unsafe everywhere, while the disconnection makes me feel like I’m floating outside my body and unable to engage with my life. Both of them severely impact my daily routine and work, so I honestly can't say which one is the main issue.\n\nDoctor: You've been experiencing these symptoms for ten days now, but can you tell me if you think the intensity or nature of your symptoms have changed at all since they first started, or have they remained relatively consistent?\n\nPatient: I'm not entirely sure, because everything has just felt like a constant blur since the shooting. It is really hard to tell if there has been any real change when I'm just feeling so overwhelmed every single day.\n\nDoctor: You've described both significant dissociative symptoms and hypervigilance since the shooting. Can you tell me if you think the dissociative feelings, such as feeling detached from yourself and your surroundings, started immediately after the shooting, or did they develop after the hypervigilance and fear began?\n\nPatient: I'm not entirely sure about the exact timeline or which symptom started first. Everything has felt like a blur since the night of the shooting, and both feelings seemed to emerge around the same time.\n\nDoctor: You've mentioned that both the dissociative feelings and hypervigilance started around the same time after the shooting, but can you try to recall if one of these symptoms was more prominent in the very first days following the incident, or did they both emerge simultaneously with equal intensity?\n\nPatient: I'm not quite sure and can't really separate them because those first few days after the shooting were such a blur. Both the constant scanning and on-edge feeling and the disconnected, movie-like feeling seemed to hit me all at once.\n\nDoctor: Given that it's been ten days since the shooting, and considering your symptoms, do you think that if the hypervigilance and fear were to decrease, the dissociative feelings of detachment would also lessen, or do you believe they are distinct issues that need to be addressed separately?\n\nPatient: I'm really not sure if the two issues are connected or separate. I haven't really thought about how they relate to each other because I'm just so overwhelmed by experiencing both of them at the same time right now.\n\nDoctor: Do you think that if you were able to manage or reduce your hypervigilance and fear, you would also experience a decrease in the feelings of detachment and disconnection from yourself and your surroundings?"

It really feels like I'm just moving through a movie of my life rather than actually living it.\n\nDoctor: Can you describe if these feelings of detachment and being in a 'movie' are more distressing or disruptive to your daily life compared to the hypervigilance and fear of something bad happening again?\n\nPatient: It's hard to say which is worse because they both severely damage my daily functioning and overall well-being in different ways.
